clue.text: Name Eden's endless downfall

wordplay.note: the crisis that ended Anthony Eden's premiership, the 1956 canal affair, with its final letter cut off

explanation.surface: A demand to identify the event that brought Eden down.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was the British Prime Minister forced out after the Suez crisis of 1956; 'Eden' looks like the garden of the Fall, but it is the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Sue is a common girl's first name, so it is an example of a name.

clue.text: A little stiff getting up, look round and pull out

indicators.note: the look word goes round the reversed stiff

parts.note: to see is to look

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: a stiff is a corpse, and dec. is the short form of deceased

explanation.surface: Someone stiffly stands, glances about and leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to withdraw formally from a union or alliance.

clue.text: Still around for some sad lives?

indicators.note: sad letters are in a sorry state and get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wistful question about whether some lonely people are still alive.
explanation.walkthrough: Some fans insist the King of Rock and Roll never died; 'Elvis lives' is their slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley, the singer some fans claim is still alive and has been sighted since 1977.

clue.text: Tank in which Posh deflowered Brenda and servant

indicators.note: a flower is a river in crosswords, so the river name is plucked out of the word Posh

parts.note: taken as written, as in Posh Spice
the Po is the great river of northern Italy
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER
a man is a manservant

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid story about Posh Spice, the Queen and a servant in some tank.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flower' in crosswords is something that flows, a river. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sherman was the main American battle tank of the Second World War.

clue.text: Pisspoor surgeon takes credit for sponging bum

indicators.note: a crude word for badly done, telling us the letters are a mess

parts.note: taken as written
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A useless surgeon gets paid for swabbing a patient's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' looks like the backside being swabbed, but here it is a layabout.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrounger lives off others, and a bum is an idle freeloader.

clue.text: Dire magazine with look of the bad speller

parts.note: evil means dreadful or dire
Private Eye, the magazine this puzzle appears in

explanation.surface: A dreadful periodical with something of the poor speller about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speller' suggests bad spelling, a dig at Private Eye's typos, but means one who casts spells.
explanation.definitionFit: The evil eye is a glance believed to cast a curse, the look of a witch.

clue.text: Explosive power rating of Jasper, say, getting an erection, upset Nato

indicators.note: in a down clue, being erected stands the letters upright, reading upwards

parts.note: jasper is a semi-precious stone, an example of a gem

indicators.note: Nato is overturned and its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the military alliance

explanation.surface: A smutty tale of a man called Jasper aroused while annoying the military alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jasper' looks like a man's name, perhaps the comedian Jasper Carrott, but is the stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A megaton is the yield of a nuclear bomb equal to a million tons of TNT.

clue.text: Not a clanger long dropped by the prize donor

indicators.note: the letter for long falls out

parts.note: a clanger is a bell, so no bell is not one
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large or long

explanation.surface: A prize-giver making no blunder in a long-winded way.
explanation.walkthrough: A clanger is British slang for a blunder; here it is a literal bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel left his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes, so he is their benefactor.

clue.text: Pleasure a woman …

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a woman's first name

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue to make a saucy sentence, but this clue stands alone as two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means delight, and it is also a woman's given name.

clue.text: Sweet girl holds in belly somehow

indicators.note: the girl's name wraps around the jumbled belly

parts.note: Jean is a girl's name

indicators.note: the letters of belly are arranged in some other way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lovely girl sucking her stomach in somehow.
explanation.definitionFit: A jelly bean is a small bean-shaped confectionery with a chewy centre.

clue.text: Oh boy! A pathetic, derisive ejaculation

indicators.note: a pathetic effort is a mess, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mocking cry about a feeble performance in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ejaculation' in its old sense is a sudden exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Yah-boo is a jeering exclamation of contempt, as in yah-boo politics.

clue.text: … very old, into humping and getting frisky

indicators.note: the very-old letters go into the word for humping

parts.note: to hump is to carry something heavy, so humping is carting

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: an aged woman being pleasured and growing lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humping' reads as the vulgar sense; here it is the British sense of lugging a load about.
explanation.definitionFit: To cavort is to leap and prance about excitedly, a lively, playful kind of behaviour.

clue.text: Blair's first encounter with topless movie star produces windy outburst

indicators.note: only the opening letter of Blair is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the name Blair

indicators.note: the top letter of the star's name is removed

parts.note: Raquel Welch, the Hollywood actress

explanation.surface: Tony Blair meets a bare-chested film actress and lets out a gust of wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests nudity, fitting Raquel Welch's pin-up image, but it just takes off the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A belch is an expulsion of gas from the stomach, a noisy release of wind.

clue.text: Be contentious — decline to swallow phlegm without hesitation

indicators.note: the word for decline takes the shortened phlegm word inside it

parts.note: to die is to fade away or decline

indicators.note: the hesitation sound is left off the phlegm word

parts.note: sputum is coughed-up phlegm
um is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A quarrelsome person refusing to swallow phlegm without pausing.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispute is to argue or contest a point, which is what being contentious means.

clue.text: Reckoning on getting mostly roasted, sets off the foxhunting fraternity

parts.note: a tally is a running count or reckoning

indicators.note: most of the word, losing its last letter

parts.note: something roasted is hot

explanation.surface: A bill that comes due over a roast sends the hunt galloping off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description, not a synonym: the call is what launches the hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Tally-ho is the cry a huntsman gives on sighting the fox, starting the chase.

clue.text: Arse-licking, ironically?

parts.note: read literally, a tongue placed on a buttock
the phrase's real meaning is said in jest, not seriously

explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally the phrase describes a tongue on a cheek, the crude picture in the first word; its everyday sense is ironic speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking with tongue in cheek means saying something insincerely or with irony.

clue.text: A drink of extreme Protestants requiring aural assistance

parts.note: members of the Orange Order, militant Ulster Protestants

indicators.note: heard rather than seen, so the help word is spelt by its sound

parts.note: aid is help

explanation.surface: Hardline Ulster loyalists needing hearing aids.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Order is a hardline Protestant fraternity in Northern Ireland, named after William of Orange.
explanation.definitionFit: Orangeade is a sweet fizzy soft drink flavoured with orange.

clue.text: Not quite pissed if there's an equal amount left in the glass

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tipsy, only partly intoxicated

definitions.text: if there's an equal amount left in the glass
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a glass with half its drink consumed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British slang for drunk, not angry; one sense is a person, the other the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes someone partly intoxicated and also a drink of which half is gone.

clue.text: Bras undone at end of parade by remarkable military force, mainly for show

indicators.note: the bra letters come apart and are refastened in another order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the final letter of parade is used

parts.note: the final letter of parade
rattling is an old-fashioned word for very good or remarkable, as in a rattling yarn

explanation.surface: Underwear comes loose at the close of a military parade.
explanation.walkthrough: Rattling as an adjective (a rattling good story) is dated British usage for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabre-rattling is a display of threatened armed force meant to intimidate rather than be used.

clue.text: Spin, etc. unfortunately required for what Blair hopes Labour supporters will do

definitions.text: what Blair hopes Labour supporters will do

parts.note: to reel is to whirl or spin

indicators.note: things going badly for the etc letters means they are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written, without the full stop

explanation.surface: New Labour's spin doctoring is a sad necessity for winning another term.
explanation.walkthrough: Written ahead of the 2001 general election, when Tony Blair sought a second term.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair wanted voters to return his government to office, choosing it again at the polls.

clue.text: Vibrator's effect — lot more excitement

indicators.note: the letters get worked up and jump around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sex toy produces a lot more arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: A vibrator here is anything that vibrates, such as a musician's vibrato.
explanation.definitionFit: Tremolo is a wavering, trembling musical effect produced by rapid repetition or vibration.

clue.text: Not up to appearing in Sun? A blessing!

indicators.note: the letters show up within the run of words

parts.note: the answer runs across the end of Sun, the A and the start of blessing

explanation.surface: A sly dig at the Sun newspaper's feeble standards.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unable to do something means lacking the capacity for it.

clue.text: Willy with scorch mark on the end of it

parts.note: a brand is a mark burnt in with hot iron

indicators.note: the last letter of the following word is added

parts.note: the last letter of it

explanation.surface: A painful injury to the private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willy' is British slang for penis, but here it is Willy Brandt, West German Chancellor 1969-74.
explanation.definitionFit: Willy Brandt was the West German statesman, the man known by that first name.

clue.text: Close couple's bedroom habit

parts.note: nigh means near or close
to tie is to couple or join together

explanation.surface: A cosy pair's usual routine between the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' looks like a routine, but it is a garment, as in a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a garment, and a nightie is a nightdress worn in bed.

clue.text: Beat heartless lover-boy

indicators.note: the word heart itself is removed from the term

parts.note: a heart-throb is an idolised handsome man

explanation.surface: A violent order to thrash a callous Romeo.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a single pulse or beat, as of the heart.

clue.text: Poor sod who has to get the software to work endures breakdown!

definitions.text: Poor sod who has to get the software to work

indicators.note: the word endures is broken down and its letters rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The hapless person stuck making the program run puts up with a crash.
explanation.definitionFit: The end-user is the person who finally operates a product, here the hapless customer of buggy software.

clue.text: Southern speed (no heroin) scam

indicators.note: the speed word is to have none of the heroin letter

parts.note: to whizz is to go fast; whizz is also slang for the drug speed

explanation.surface: A drug deal down south: amphetamines cut with no heroin, a con.
explanation.walkthrough: Speed and whizz are both slang for amphetamine, the drugs reading of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A swizz is informal British for a swindle or disappointing con.

clue.text: Brown's first to retreat from him?

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for the man Brown served under

indicators.note: only the opening letter of Brown is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the name Brown
a lair is an animal's den or hideaway

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's main wish to get away from his rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Written in 2001, when Gordon Brown was Chancellor and famously at odds with Tony Blair, the Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'him' Brown would most want to escape from was his political rival and boss of the day.

clue.text: Well executed speech — cert to wriggle out of the chair's purpose

indicators.note: the reordered cert letters escape from the longer word

parts.note: the electric chair exists for electrocution
the letters of cert squirm into the order they take inside the longer word

explanation.surface: A condemned man's polished final words as he tries to escape the electric chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Executed' points to the electric chair but works in the definition as well performed.
explanation.definitionFit: Elocution is the skill of clear, expressive speaking, so good elocution is well-delivered speech.

clue.text: Dick's fortnightly treat

parts.note: a dick is American slang for a detective, a private investigator
the satirical magazine that prints this puzzle comes out every two weeks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' tempts towards the vulgar reading, as befits this magazine, but means a detective, a private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine published every fortnight, and a private eye is a detective.

clue.text: Not a complete arse, however sound

parts.note: but means however
tock is the sound of a clock, as in tick-tock

explanation.surface: A grudging compliment: someone is not entirely a fool, though they look it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arse' looks like the insult for a fool; it is the literal backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A buttock is one cheek of the backside, only half of the whole bottom.

clue.text: An adolescent outburst, being the last to have sex?

parts.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A teenager's tantrum about being the last of the gang to lose their virginity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outburst' suggests a tantrum, but it is a spot breaking out on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A zit is a pimple, the kind of skin eruption typical of teenagers.
